newsitem.title: USA: Calif. spring runoff forecast much above average.
newsitem.headline: Calif. spring runoff forecast much above average.

text.p: California's stream runoff will total well above historic levels this spring, with most of the excess in the southern portion of the Sierra Nevada mountains, according to the California Department of Water Resources' (DWR) first official forecast for 1997.

The southern Sierras will see the heaviest runoff since recent storms were largely concentrated at higher elevations, while most of the precipitation in northern regions was in the form of rain, Frank Gehrke at the DWR snow survey center said.

The state agency forecast April-July runoff on the Feather River at 120 percent of average, with the Yuba River runoff forecast at 130 percent of average and the San Joaquin River at 180 percent of normal levels.

Most of Pacific Gas and Electric Co's hydroelectric projects are in central and northern portions of the mountains, while Southern California Edison Co's hydropower operations on the San Joaquin River.
"There is a substantial increase in anticipated runoff as you move further south," Gehrke said.
He explained that maximum elevation in the southern Sierras is 10,000 to 12,000 feet, compared with 8,000 feet at the northern end of the mountain range.
"We had a lot of storms at 9,000 feet this year, so there is more snow in the south. Quite often this is the opposite, but the rain in the northern Sierras was immediate runoff," Gehrke noted.
Water content of snowpack in the northern Sierras stands at 97 percent of average, while the central Sierrras have 157 percent and the southern areas have 185 percent, the state agency said.
Statewide snowpack is 145 percent of average, compared with 97 percent at this time last year, Gehrke said.

During January-October of last year, hydroelectricity accounted for 39 percent ot total California power generation, compared with 41 percent in the same 1995 period, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).

Over the last 15 years, hydropower's share of the state's overall generation has ranged from 49 percent in 1983 to a negative 19.3 percent in 1990 when a drought led hydropower projects to consume more energy than they produced.
In the Northwest, the National Weather Service's River Forecast Center last estimated January-July runoff at The Dalles dam on the Columbia River at 137 percent of average.
Last year, runoff at The Dalles totaled 132 percent of the 30-year average or 139.3 million acre feet (maf).
The 1996 runoff total was the largest since 1974 and the fourth largest in 66 years of record-keeping, the center said.
Hydropower represents the largest source of electricity in the Pacific Northwest, and above-average precipitation can push the total close to two-thirds of overall generation.
In 1983, hydropower accounted for 72 percent of electricity output in Washington, Oregon and California, compared with 9.5 percent in 1990.
